standard.title: Drama across cultures, times and places
standard.description: explore where, why and how drama is created and/or performed across cultures, times, places and/or other contexts
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can explore where, why and how people across cultures experience drama (Y1-2). They understand that drama communicates feelings, ideas and cultural knowledge for different communities.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explore where, why and how drama is created and/or performed across cultures, times, places and other contexts.

nodes.label: Purpose and audience across contexts
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify the purpose of a drama — entertainment, cultural transmission, infotainment, community ritual — and describe what an audience needs to know to engage with it.
nodes.minimum_width: Student identifies one purpose for a specific drama they have experienced or studied, and names one thing an audience needs to understand.
nodes.typical_width: Students listen to actors or makers discuss how they developed characters and what they found interesting about the imaginary world they created; they reflect on live or recorded performances asking what purpose the drama serves; they compare expectations and requirements of performers and audience in different cultural settings.
wider: Students compare a drama from Australia with one from a country or region in Asia, identifying similarities and differences in purpose and audience relationship
Students examine puppetry or physical theatre in their community and compare it with examples from other cultures, times or places
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding purpose and audience is prerequisite to the analytical inquiry asked by the descriptor — 'how drama is created/performed' is only interpretable if students have a frame for 'why'; without it, observation stays at surface description.

response_modes.reason: Use structured reflection questions before and after viewing drama: 'What is the purpose of this drama?', 'What does the audience need to know?', 'Why do you think people from this culture create drama for this purpose?'

success_criteria: Student identifies a purpose for a specific drama from a given cultural context
Student describes at least one thing an audience needs to know to engage with that drama

nodes.label: Features and ideas across cultures, times and places
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify features and ideas in drama from diverse cultures, times and places, and consider how they might inform their own drama-making.
nodes.minimum_width: Student identifies one feature or idea from a drama from another culture, time or place and considers how it might be used in their own work.
nodes.typical_width: Students reflect on drama performances and ask questions ('What features and ideas come from other cultures, times and places?', 'How could we use these in our drama?', 'Why do people from diverse cultures create drama for similar purposes?'); they share embodied responses — movement, gesture, language — to reflect on drama meaning.
wider: Students investigate a specific drama form from another culture or historical period in depth — exploring its conventions, purposes and how it has changed over time
Students investigate how drama from a country or region in Asia uses elements differently from Australian dramatic conventions and apply one insight in their own devising

response_modes.reason: Exposure to a range of drama contexts, times and cultures is the mechanism here; breadth of examples enables comparison and supports genuine understanding of drama's diversity.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The range of cultural, historical and contextual drama examples available for exploration is very wide; students who engage across multiple examples develop stronger comparative and analytical capabilities.
success_criteria: Student identifies at least one feature or idea in drama from a cultural or historical context different from their own
Student makes a connection between that feature and their own drama-making practice or ideas
